title: OpenAI says an internal model produced new results in math, CS and physics
subtitle: The company published 722 machine-generated manuscripts organized into 372 research families — including a claim that the local smoothing conjecture now has a proof in every spatial dimension — and formalized many of the proofs in Lean so outside readers can check them.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: OpenAI announced on October 27 that an internal, unpublished reasoning model has produced a set of new research results across pure mathematics, theoretical computer science, and mathematical physics. The release spans three headline areas: harmonic analysis, complexity theory, and quantum field theory. The company put the full output into a public repository of 722 manuscripts, organized into 372 research families, and formalized many of the proofs in the Lean 4 proof assistant so computers can mechanically check the arguments. In harmonic analysis, OpenAI claims the model produced a proof of the local smoothing conjecture in every spatial dimension — a longstanding open problem connected to the Kakeya, Bochner-Riesz, and restriction conjectures.

The scale is the point, not any single result. 722 is more than any individual mathematician could produce in a career, and the whole corpus landed at once with uniform notation and Lean checks. OpenAI said in its own release that some of the unverified work may contain errors, and that outside mathematicians will need to inspect the output before anything is accepted into the literature. That is a careful framing: Lean verification shows a proof follows from stated premises, but it does not catch a model that quietly rewrote a well-known earlier proof under new notation and called it novel.

The announcement comes against a run of similar claims that have cooled off on contact with experts. OpenAI's May disproof of a planar unit distance conjecture was partially validated. A September Navier-Stokes claim has not been. A separate Harmonic/Aristotle Erdős result from earlier this year was walked back after Terence Tao and others pointed out it relied on widely known methods, and OpenAI's Kevin Weil deleted a victory-lap post. The 722-paper drop is in part a response to that pattern — releasing the artifacts and the Lean files together, instead of a press release, is an invitation for external verification before claims harden.

A note for learners: formal verification is the signal to watch. A chain of reasoning that type-checks in Lean is not automatically a mathematical breakthrough, but it is a mathematical object a human can inspect line by line, and it rules out the sloppiest failure modes (circular arguments, hand-waved steps, miscited lemmas). If you want to understand what AI-generated math is actually worth right now, learn enough Lean or Rocq to open one of these proof files and read it. The gap between what a reasoning model asserts and what a proof assistant will accept is where the next few years of this field will be won or lost.
